subject: British History
title: 7. Industrial and Agricultural Revolutions and Their Political-Social Effects

segments.text: Industrialisation should be explained as a connected system of reinforcing changes, not a single invention or “magic factor” — and its social and political consequences (new classes, new cities, new political movements) are as testable as its economic causes.

blocks.text: Transport, Urbanisation, and New Social Classes

segments.text: Canals, turnpike roads, and later railways sharply reduced transport costs and connected regional markets, while Britain’s overseas trade and empire supplied both raw materials and export customers. Rapid urban growth created new industrial cities, a growing middle class, and an expanding wage-earning working class, with housing, sanitation, disease, and workplace conditions becoming major social and political questions in their own right — not side effects to be mentioned only in passing.

Prepare causes as an interconnected system, not one single factor; build a consequences table covering economy, urban society, labour, politics, ideas, public health and empire.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “How did industrialisation produce new political movements and demands in early nineteenth-century Britain?”
Do not search for one single cause of industrialisation; it was a connected system of changes.
Do not say enclosure automatically created industrial workers everywhere; the relationship varied regionally.
Do not treat industrialisation as only economic progress; social cost and political conflict are essential to the topic.
Agricultural change included enclosure, crop rotation, selective breeding and commercialisation, with timing and effects varying by region.
Coal, iron, mechanised textiles and steam power were central to early British industrialisation.
Rapid urban growth produced both opportunity and severe housing, sanitation and labour problems.
Chartism, especially from the late 1830s, demanded broader male suffrage and other parliamentary changes.
Present industrialisation as a system of mutually reinforcing changes (agriculture, energy, technology, transport, markets) rather than any single cause.
New social classes and new political movements (Chartism, trade unions) are direct consequences of industrial change and belong in the same answer as the economic narrative, not a separate one.
